Clouds and Sunshine: Separation and the Possibility of Return On Rabindranath Tagore’s “Megh O Roudra”

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-11-18

In Rabindranath Tagore’s “Megh O Roudra” (“Clouds and Sunshine”), the relationship between Shashibhushan and Giribala begins with an apparently modest exchange: a young man teaches a little girl to read. Yet what develops between them gradually acquires a significance that reaches far beyond the intimacy of a village household. Their companionship unfolds within a society governed by inherited authority, colonial power, social prejudice, and the quiet submission of those who have learned that resistance may come at a considerable cost. The story’s emotional centre is therefore inseparable from its moral and political world. What appears at first to be a tale of affection and separation becomes, in time, an examination of the ways in which power enters ordinary lives, distorts human relationships, and leaves its consequences long after the immediate conflict has passed.

Shashibhushan is an educated young man with an M.A. and a B.L. degree, but his education has done little to secure him a recognised place in village society. Short-sighted, withdrawn, and inclined to live within the world of his books, he is regarded with a mixture of incomprehension and indifference. His learning, instead of making him socially influential, seems to set him apart. He possesses a strong sense of justice, but the community around him has little use for a form of integrity that refuses to accommodate convenience. It is through his association with Giribala, his young neighbour, that another aspect of his character emerges. She is eight when their acquaintance begins and later reaches the age of ten. Her brothers show little interest in her intellectual curiosity, but Shashibhushan takes it seriously. He teaches her to read, and the lessons gradually become the occasion for a companionship that neither of them quite knows how to define.

There is something especially revealing about the place of reading in this relationship. For Giribala, the primer opens a world that the restrictions of her domestic life have scarcely allowed her to imagine. For Shashibhushan, teaching her offers a form of human contact that his isolation elsewhere has denied him. Their relationship is neither an ordinary friendship between equals nor simply that of a teacher and pupil. It develops through small, repeated acts of attention: the arrival of the girl, the opening of a book, the progress of a lesson, the pleasure of discovering that another person is genuinely interested in what one has to offer. The importance of these moments becomes clearer only when they are taken away. Tagore does not need to make the relationship dramatic at its beginning; its quietness is precisely what gives the later separation its force.

The first serious disturbance comes from the world of adult authority. Giribala’s father, Harkumar, is a former landholder who now serves as a zamindari naib. He is accustomed to the practical calculations of power and property. Shashibhushan, however, refuses to assist him in cases involving coercion against a tenant. This refusal exposes a difference between the two men that is more fundamental than a disagreement over professional advice. Harkumar regards authority as something to be exercised in the service of established interests; Shashibhushan sees no reason to lend his education to an injustice merely because it has the support of those who command it. His refusal is principled, but it also makes him inconvenient.

The conflict becomes more acute when a British Joint Magistrate humiliates Harkumar over an alleged failure to supply ghee for the magistrate’s dog. The incident is at once petty and revealing. The colonial officer’s authority is so secure that even an ordinary domestic demand can become an occasion for public humiliation. Harkumar, who occupies a position of authority within the local hierarchy, discovers that his own power is insignificant when measured against that of the British official. Shashibhushan offers to bring a case against the magistrate for defamation. In doing so, he treats the insult as an injury that can and should be answered through the law. But Harkumar is unable to sustain that position. Fear of the consequences, concern for his standing, and the desire to protect his own interests overcome whatever sense of grievance he may have felt. He withdraws the case and, in an act of self-preservation, identifies Shashibhushan as a Congress agitator.

This episode reveals one of the story’s central ironies. The law, which ought to provide a means of redress against arbitrary authority, becomes uncertain in the hands of people who are unwilling to bear the cost of invoking it. Shashibhushan believes that an injustice should be challenged because it is an injustice. Harkumar believes that the practical consequences of such a challenge must be calculated before any action is taken. Neither position exists in a social vacuum. The colonial administration has created an order in which the powerful can act with impunity, while those below them are encouraged to preserve themselves by yielding, retreating, or transferring the burden of danger to someone else. Harkumar’s conduct is therefore more than a personal betrayal. It is an expression of a wider social habit: the habit of accommodating injustice when resistance threatens one's own security.

Yet the public conflict has consequences within a much smaller and more intimate world. Shashibhushan becomes absorbed in the case and gradually neglects Giribala. The girl, who had once found in him an attentive companion, experiences his withdrawal as a personal rejection. She does not possess the maturity to understand the larger circumstances that have occupied him, nor does she have the freedom to demand an explanation. Her response is painfully simple. She stops visiting him and tears up her primer. The destruction of the book is more than a childish gesture of anger. The primer had been the material sign of their companionship; to tear it is, in her limited understanding, to reject the relationship that has suddenly become inaccessible to her.

The episode also suggests how easily a public struggle can damage private affections, even when those affections have nothing to do with the conflict itself. Shashibhushan is engaged in a contest over justice, but he fails to recognise that the girl who has come to depend on his attention is experiencing another kind of injustice: the unexplained disappearance of someone important to her. The story does not present him as morally diminished by this failure. Rather, it allows us to see the limitations of a character whose ethical seriousness is not always accompanied by an equal understanding of emotional need. His concern for justice is genuine, but it does not protect him from causing pain through inattention.

Harkumar soon arranges Giribala’s marriage and prevents her from visiting Shashibhushan. The decision belongs to the familiar machinery of family authority, in which a girl’s wishes carry little weight against the arrangements made by her elders. Giribala’s education, her attachment to her teacher, and the small world they have created together are all set aside without discussion. Shashibhushan eventually leaves the village. On the day of Giribala’s wedding, he sees her boat departing. She does not see him. He watches her leave and weeps, while she remains unaware of his presence.

The separation is especially affecting because it is not produced by a single decisive confrontation. No one announces the end of their relationship; no final conversation gives it shape or meaning. It disappears through a sequence of ordinary decisions made by people who possess the power to determine the lives of others. A father arranges a marriage, a girl is prevented from visiting, a young man leaves the village, and a boat carries a bride away. The emotional weight of the scene lies in the distance between what Shashibhushan sees and what Giribala does not know. He witnesses the departure of someone who has become essential to his inner life, but the person departing has no knowledge that she is being watched. Their separation is complete precisely because it is so unequal in awareness.

The story might have remained a personal tragedy had Tagore not widened its field of vision. On his journey by river, Shashibhushan witnesses an episode that exposes the violence of colonial authority in a more direct and brutal form. A British steamer manager, angered because a local merchant’s boat has overtaken the steamer, fires at its sail. The boat sinks. Shashibhushan helps rescue those on board, but one of the crew, the cook, is missing and is later found dead. The manager is acquitted, despite admitting that he fired the shot and offering an explanation that scarcely justifies what he has done. The local people refuse to testify.

The incident is disturbing not merely because a man has been killed, but because the institutions that should establish responsibility fail to do so. The manager’s position protects him; the victims’ social weakness leaves them exposed. The witnesses understand the danger of speaking against a European official and choose silence. Their refusal is not difficult to explain. They have learned, through experience or observation, that truth does not necessarily prevail in a court where power has already determined the relative value of the people involved. Yet the result is devastating. A man is dead, the person responsible escapes punishment, and the community participates in the concealment of the crime through its fear.

Shashibhushan cannot accept this arrangement. What he has witnessed is intolerable to him because it violates the most elementary distinction between right and wrong. But his sense of justice repeatedly brings him into conflict with a world in which justice is treated as a matter of influence, position, and expediency. The episode on the river is thus connected to the earlier humiliation of Harkumar. In both cases, a British official exercises power arbitrarily; in both, the people who suffer the consequences discover that the ordinary instruments of redress offer little protection. The difference lies in the scale of the violence and in the response of those who witness it. Harkumar retreats to preserve himself. The boatmen remain silent to avoid danger. Shashibhushan alone insists that the event must be answered.

A later encounter with the police superintendent brings this conflict to its conclusion. Shashibhushan sees the officer cutting the fishermen’s expensive net and detaining men without proper justification. When he protests, the superintendent insults him. Shashibhushan attacks the officer and is arrested. At the trial, fishermen and other witnesses withdraw or alter their accounts. Some are frightened; others may have their own reasons for avoiding involvement. Harkumar, too, is implicated in the betrayal that helps secure Shashibhushan’s conviction. He receives a sentence of five years.

The pattern is now unmistakable. The colonial officer can commit an act of violence and remain beyond the reach of punishment; the ordinary people who witness the event can protect themselves by refusing to speak; the man who insists on confronting the injustice is left to face the law alone. Shashibhushan’s conduct may be impulsive, and his assault on the superintendent cannot simply be treated as a legal or political solution. But Tagore makes it difficult to regard the punishment as an adequate expression of justice. The formal proceedings have taken place, witnesses have spoken, and a sentence has been pronounced. What remains absent is any credible relationship between the judgment of the court and the truth of what happened.

Shashibhushan refuses to appeal. His explanation is one of the most revealing statements in the story: the iron restraints of prison, he says, do not lie, whereas the freedom outside can deceive. The remark is bitter, but its bitterness has been earned. Prison offers a visible and acknowledged form of confinement. The world beyond its walls claims to be free, yet its freedom is sustained by false testimony, fear, betrayal, and the unequal distribution of power. The prisoner knows that he is imprisoned; the supposedly free society refuses to acknowledge the chains by which it is governed. In this sense, Shashibhushan’s refusal to appeal is not simply an act of resignation. It is also a judgment on the moral condition of the world that has condemned him.

During his imprisonment, his father dies, and Harkumar appropriates most of his property. When Shashibhushan emerges after five years, he has lost almost everything that might have connected him to his former life. He has no home in any meaningful sense, no family waiting for him, and no secure place in the community. The punishment has extended far beyond the sentence imposed by the court. Five years have passed, but the damage cannot be measured by the duration of his imprisonment. The social world to which he might have returned has been altered, and the relationships that once gave his life meaning have been broken or dispersed.

It is at this point that the story begins to move towards its final and unexpected convergence. A carriage brings Shashibhushan to a mansion. Inside, he finds books and familiar school materials: his old slate, primer, exercise books, and a copy of the Mahabharata. On them is the name “Giribala Devi,” written in his own hand. The objects have survived the years of separation and the upheavals that have transformed both their lives. Their presence is more eloquent than any explanation could be. The books recall a time when Giribala was a child learning to read, when Shashibhushan’s attention was still part of her daily life, and when their companionship seemed so ordinary that neither could have imagined its disappearance.

These objects perform an important function in the story. They are not merely sentimental reminders of the past. They are material evidence that the relationship has continued to exist in some form, even after the people themselves have been separated. The primer that Giribala once tore up in anger belongs to the beginning of their estrangement; the surviving books now make possible a recognition that neither time nor circumstance has entirely erased their connection. The name written on them links the two periods of their lives. It also gives Shashibhushan a first indication that the girl he once taught has not forgotten him.

Meanwhile, a group of kirtan singers is performing nearby. Their song contains the repeated appeal, “ফিরে এসো”—come back. Shashibhushan finds himself continuing the song inwardly, adding to its refrain from within the storehouse of his own memories. The music and the objects begin to work upon him together. The words of return, which might otherwise belong to a devotional or communal performance, acquire a deeply personal meaning. They seem to address not merely an absent person but an entire lost world: the village, the lessons, the childhood companionship, and the life that might have been.

The final appearance of Giribala transforms this recognition into an encounter. She is now a widow. The child who once came to Shashibhushan with a primer has grown into a woman whose life has been shaped by circumstances over which she had little control. She brings him food and bows before him. Neither can find the words that might adequately express what has happened between them. They weep.

The scene is moving because Tagore does not attempt to resolve their history through explanation. There is no extended conversation in which Giribala recounts her life or Shashibhushan describes the years he has lost. The story allows the recognition to take place through gesture, presence, and tears. The old relationship returns, but it cannot return unchanged. The child and the teacher no longer occupy the world in which their companionship began. Both have passed through experiences that cannot be undone. What remains possible is a form of recognition that accepts the distance between the past and the present without pretending that the distance has never existed.

The kirtan singers continue their song, and the final words—“এসো এসো হে!”—give the ending its particular resonance. The repeated invitation to return is at once musical, devotional, and emotional. It gathers into a single refrain the different meanings of homecoming that the story has been preparing: the return of a person, the recovery of a memory, the renewal of a broken human connection, and perhaps the possibility that something of the past may still be preserved within the present. The song does not erase the suffering that has preceded it. Shashibhushan has lost five years of his life, his father, his property, and his place in society. Giribala has passed through a marriage and widowhood that have left their own marks. Their meeting cannot restore what has been taken from either of them. Yet it makes possible an acknowledgment that the years of separation have not rendered their earlier affection meaningless.

The title, “Megh O Roudra,” acquires its full significance in this movement between loss and return. Clouds and sunshine are not simply descriptions of weather; they provide an emotional frame for the story. The alternation between them reflects the instability of human experience, in which moments of warmth and intimacy are repeatedly interrupted by forces that seem beyond individual control. The opening and closing images bring the narrative into a kind of formal balance, but this balance should not be mistaken for a simple reconciliation. The sunshine at the end does not cancel the clouds that have gathered over the lives of the characters. Rather, it appears through them, as something fragile and momentary that has survived despite everything.

What makes the story enduring is the way Tagore brings together two apparently separate forms of suffering. One belongs to the public world of colonial injustice, where authority is protected by institutions and ordinary people are compelled to choose between truth and safety. The other belongs to the private world of human attachment, where affection can be broken by social arrangements, parental authority, misunderstanding, and the passage of time. Shashibhushan’s tragedy lies partly in the fact that he encounters both forms of injustice without possessing the power to overcome either. His moral independence isolates him from society, while his emotional inattention contributes to the loss of the one relationship that might have offered him a refuge from that isolation.

Giribala’s position is different but no less revealing. Her life is governed by decisions made by others, first as a child whose education is treated as an indulgence and later as a young woman whose marriage is arranged without regard to her attachment or wishes. The story gives her comparatively little control over the events that determine her future. Yet her preservation of Shashibhushan’s books suggests a private continuity that the social world has failed to recognise. The objects she keeps become the silent record of a relationship that could not be sustained openly but was never entirely abandoned in memory.

In the end, “Megh O Roudra” is not simply a story about two people who are separated and eventually meet again. It is about the moral cost of living in a society where power repeatedly escapes accountability, where fear makes witnesses unreliable, and where personal lives are shaped by decisions taken in the name of authority or social respectability. It is also about the persistence of affection in circumstances that seem designed to extinguish it. Tagore does not offer a triumphant restoration of justice, nor does he suggest that emotional reunion can compensate for every loss. His ending is quieter and more difficult than that. It allows two lives, altered by suffering and time, to recognise one another again. The clouds have not disappeared; the sunshine has returned, but it falls upon a world that cannot be made whole.
